what: A steadily turning tiled platter drives an unmotorized rubber wheel. Motor B moves the wheel across the platter: forward, slower, near neutral, then reverse. The accumulated wheel angle demonstrates mechanical integration: it remembers the signed contact radius over the platter's motion. A continuously rotating tiled disk drives a free rubber wheel. Move the wheel through the center to vary its speed and reverse its direction. Gravity supplies contact pressure; the wheel is not motorized. The native recording measures finite-width slip.
try: Reset and run the bounded demonstration. Motor A spins the platter in one direction while Motor B visits +28, +14, 0 and −28 mm contact offsets. Each station lasts 6 seconds; the recorded native program finishes in about 35.7 seconds.
Compare the positive-radius stations. At +14 mm, the passive wheel turns at about half the platter's angular speed; at +28 mm, it is close to the same speed.
Watch the centre carefully. Ideal point contact predicts zero speed, but the delivered native recording shows 15.92 degrees of creep during its final 4.97 seconds. Near neutral is not an exact stop.
At the negative-radius station, the output reverses while the platter keeps its direction. The wheel has no motor or transmission constraint that imposes this rotation.
Compare the measured wheel angle with the ideal integral in the validation data. Keep the transitions visible: shifting the tyre sideways introduces scrub and transient error.
why: At fixed radius x, the platter's local surface speed is proportional to x. A tyre of radius R rolls at the corresponding angular speed, giving the ideal signed ratio wheel speed / platter speed = x/R. Crossing the centre changes the sign. Accumulating that speed makes output angle proportional to the integral of x over actual platter angle. The gravity-loaded fork also moves slightly, so the full reference includes its measured tangential centre displacement. Contact width, drag, slip and sideways scrub cause departures from the ideal relation.
matters: This is the principle of a wheel-and-disc mechanical integrator and a continuously variable friction drive. It adds a different operation to Mean Machine's differential average: the changing contact radius weights each increment of input rotation. The native contact run passed the predeclared behavior and position bounds. These numerical results concern native simulation; browser integration requires separate evidence, and physical hardware accuracy has not been established.
question: After one platter turn at x = +28 mm with a 28 mm tyre radius, you move the wheel back to the centre. Does its accumulated output angle reset to zero?
answer: No. Under ideal rolling, the first platter turn adds one wheel turn. Moving to the centre changes the subsequent rate; it does not erase the accumulated angle. An equal opposite signed integral, for example one platter turn at −28 mm, would ideally cancel it. Actual contact and transition motion introduce error.
further: Compare with Mean Machine: distinguish an instantaneous average of angles from an angle accumulated through a variable ratio.
Use actual platter angle and the tyre centre when predicting output. A bearing hinge can lie beside the tyre on the same axle; it is not the radial contact centre.

The independent pose fit measured wheel/platter ratios of +0.9963, +0.5053, +0.0395, -1.0045. The full-run final angle differed from the ideal measured-motion reference by +7.85 degrees. Inspect the complete residual alongside the ideal reference.

A separate native counterfactual used direct input controllers rather than the main Scratch VM program. Changing only the output body's friction to zero reduced its mean speed ratio from +1.0035 to -0.0041, with contact still present. This supports friction-driven sustained rotation; the frictionless wheel still oscillates, and the test does not establish a real hardware friction coefficient.

Brown's mechanical movement 28 describes the historical variable-radius friction-wheel arrangement: https://507movements.com/mm_028.html. The addon supplies an original LEGO arrangement and copies no modern site animation.

Separate actual-browser recordings passed 18 pose/program checks each, from the catalog and after saving and reopening the .sb3 project. The browser mirror exposes no rolling load, so these checks provide program and pose evidence only. Saved coordinates retain the application's normal serialization rounding and are checked against an independent compile of the exact saved text.
formula: Fixed-radius ideal: φ̇/θ̇ = x/R. Integrated ideal: Δφ = (∫x dθ)/R. With tangential fork motion: Δφ = (∫x dθ + Δz)/R. R = 28 mm; angles are signed, and wheel angle is measured relative to the support.
